activities.anchor: the future is a design decision
activities.caption: bet before you read on — who is the format for?
activities.name: dfilesFuturePredict

config.q: When you pick the format for a dataset, which reader matters most?
choices: You, or a colleague, ten years from now — with whatever software exists then
Only the program that wrote it
Whoever owns the most expensive spreadsheet
config.why: A dataset outlives the session that made it; the format is a promise about who can still open it — plain, standard formats keep that promise.

activities.anchor: read a UTF-8 file with the older Latin-1 interpretation and
activities.caption: file each fact under the encoding it describes
activities.name: dfilesEncSort

config.prompt: Byte-story facts — sort each under the encoding it describes:

items.label: one catalogue for every character in every language, plus emoji
English letters, digits and punctuation in single bytes
rarer characters spill into two, three or four bytes
useless for the rest of the world's writing systems
backward-compatible: the old single-byte characters kept their codes

config.why: The modern default kept the old single-byte range unchanged and gave every rarer character room — that is why it won.

activities.caption: true or false — what 'plain text' really is
activities.name: dfilesPlainJudge

statements.s: Every text file stores byte numbers; characters appear only when reader and writer agree on a decoding table.
statements.why: The mojibake symptom is disagreement, not damage.

statements.s: 'Plain text' needs no decisions — letters are simply stored as letters.
statements.why: There is always an encoding; the only question is whether it was chosen deliberately.

statements.s: Mojibake means the bytes are damaged and need a repair tool.
statements.why: The bytes are intact; agree on the encoding and the text reads fine.

statements.s: One encoding now rules almost everywhere because it keeps English text unchanged and covers every writing system.
statements.why: Backward compatible and complete — one decision, made once.

activities.anchor: In memory, a program holds this as an array of records (or objects)
activities.caption: design the dataset — grain and atomicity as decisions
activities.name: dfilesGrainBranch

config.root: You are designing the weather dataset from the paragraph — one row per what?

start.text: You have daily readings for 40 weather stations over ten years: temperature, rainfall, wind.

choices.label: One row per station — 40 rows, 3,650 columns
choices.feedback: Every new year means rebuilding the schema; comparing two days means leaping across hundreds of columns.

choices.label: One row per station per day
choices.feedback: 1,460,000 rows, nine columns — tall, uniform, and every tool from spreadsheets to SQL handles it the same way.

choices.label: One file per station, format chosen per station
choices.feedback: Forty formats means forty parsers; the analysis now starts with an archaeology dig.

wide.text: The wide layout works until the first schema change.

choices.label: Try adding hourly readings
choices.feedback: 24 more columns per day — the table now has a shape nobody wants to query.

choices.label: Restart with one row per station per day
choices.feedback: The tall layout absorbs new dates, new stations and new fields without touching the schema.

wideWorse.text: The table sprawls: one station's year is a row of 8,760 mostly-empty cells. Analysis tools were built for tall tables — and so were you.

grain.text: The grain is set. Now the address field: "12 Collingwood Rd, Bristol" in one column.

choices.label: Keep it as one field — it reads fine
choices.feedback: Sorting by city or deduplicating by street now needs string surgery on every row.

choices.label: Split house, street, city into separate fields
choices.feedback: Three boring columns; every future query gets to be a simple comparison.

crammed.text: The crammed field works until the first "group by city" — which becomes a parse-and-pray operation over 1.4 million rows.

atomic.text: Atomic fields, one clean grain — the dataset now survives new years, new stations and new questions.

fragile.text: Per-station formats trade one design decision for forty. Consistency is the cheaper contract.

config.why: Grain first, atomicity second: one row per what decides everything downstream, and one-value-per-field keeps every future query trivial.

activities.anchor: silently shifting every column after it
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the plain table's traps
activities.name: dfilesCsvSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about the plain-table format is backwards — click it:
lines: CSV is plain text: openable in any editor, spreadsheet or language, with no software dependency.
CSV has no opinion on types — each reader re-decides what "34" is.
Spreadsheets are careful with guesses: leading zeros on barcodes are always preserved.
Some countries export semicolon-CSV because the comma is their decimal point.
Line endings differ between Windows and Unix.
So a CSV travels with a schema note: which separator, which encoding, what each attribute means and holds.
config.correction: The guesses mangle: leading zeros vanish from barcodes, long account numbers become floating point, "3/4" turns into a date.
config.why: Type-blindness is the price of universality — the schema note is the apology that travels with it.

activities.anchor: so bank-account or product IDs are exchanged as strings
activities.caption: two formats, two philosophies — drag the divider
activities.name: dfilesCsvJsonCompare

config.prompt: One table, two philosophies — drag the divider:

before.label: CSV
before.text: positional columns in plain text — universal, type-blind, simplest when the table is wide and flat

after.label: JSON
after.text: labels travel with values and objects nest in arrays — the lingua franca of web APIs

config.why: Wide and flat → positions; nested and labelled → names. Mind the edges: dates are text, huge integers lose precision, trailing commas are illegal.

activities.anchor: It answers the questions every future reader has
activities.caption: pair each promise with the clause that keeps it
activities.name: dfilesSchemaMatch

config.prompt: Pair each promise with the clause that keeps it:

pairs.right: unknown, not-applicable or zero — declared, never guessed
metres or centimetres — the 1999 orbiter was lost mixing pound-seconds with newton-seconds
student_id a unique integer; name text; submitted true or false

config.why: A promise about meaning and types — the ten-year test judges whether it survives.

activities.anchor: whole file at once, or line by line for big files
activities.caption: processing a table from disk — the canonical pattern
activities.name: dfilesReadOrder

config.prompt: The canonical read-a-table pattern, in order:
items: Open for reading — name the path and the mode
Use or skip the header row
Loop over the rows, splitting each into fields
Convert types and accumulate — totals, counts, bests
Close the handle — buffered data dies if you never do
config.why: Open, read, close — plus the robustness habits: the blank last row, the quoted comma, the value that should be a number but is 'N/A'.
